x.name: alphaXiv
x.bio: High fidelity research

tweets.text:
"A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets"

RL can actually make an LLM forget how to generate its best answers, even while its average reward continues improving.

This paper identifies a phenomenon called coverage collapse, where policy optimization slowly reduces the probability of generating optimal responses, making them increasingly difficult to rediscover during training.

They then proposed Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), which repeatedly resets the KL reference to the latest model instead of always using the original base model. This lets RL to make controlled improvements while continuing to move toward better solutions.

Reference resets provide stronger convergence guarantees for simplified PPO, GRPO, and Kimi-style algorithms too.

https://t.co/r7BC6FZqEs

"The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training"

LLMs can learn entirely new capabilities by simply deleting less than 0.05% of their pretrained weights, without modifying any of the remaining parameters...?

This new paper proposes Deletion Tuning, which learns a binary mask that determines which weights to remove from the model's feedforward layers. Unlike conventional fine-tuning or LoRA, it doesn't learn new weight values, but instead learns which existing connections to disable.

Across RL, SFT, and distillation, Deletion Tuning matches full fine-tuning at the largest scales tested. 

On a 30B-parameter model, it achieves 58.54% vs 58.43% for full fine-tuning, with an adapter roughly 4,000x smaller. 

It also preserves previous capabilities better, while conventional fine-tuning methods lose up to 5.4% of prior-task accuracy.

The reason this might work is because full fine-tuning tends to preserve the model's main weight structure while making changes outside its dominant components. So selectively deleting a tiny fraction of weights can produce a similar pattern of changes without disturbing the rest of the model.

https://t.co/UB4aoYcFGW

As open models approach the frontier, so too will their research capabilities.

x.name: Guillermo Rauch
x.bio: @vercel CEO

tweets.text:
What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? 

The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate.

UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously. 

Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine.

I think we've found someone that allows us to have the cake and eat it too. A decades-long dream. UI SDK is packaged behaviors that give us accessibility, performance, cohesion, saving us tokens, errors and effort, but with absolutely zero limitations and tradeoffs for what UIs we can generate.

Enjoy!
